title: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Migration and isolation do not by themselves cause modification; a group of competing species that migrates together into a new, isolated country will be little modified, because modification is driven by organisms being brought into new relations with one another.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If, for instance, a number of species, which stand in direct competition with each other, migrate in a body into a new and afterwards isolated country, they will be little liable to modification; for neither migration nor isolation in themselves can do anything.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Affinity of the productions of the same continent”. Scope: species colonising new isolated areas

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism has measurable consequences, but relevant natural experiments are scattered and rarely isolate the proposed cause. Existing data can test case studies, not the broad counterfactual.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare phenotypic and genomic change after isolated colonization by intact multi-species assemblages versus single or compositionally disrupted colonists, controlling time and environment. Support requires little change in intact-group colonizations and more change when biotic relations shift.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Migration changes abiotic conditions as well as species interactions.

Intact community colonizations are rare and poorly replicated.

'Little modified' lacks a universal scale.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.65
data existence: 0.66
discriminating power: 0.35
data adequacy: 0.39
analysis feasibility: 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast between a co-immigrating assemblage and a singleton colonist is a real comparative prediction, but the arrival mode is not a column in open databases. Trees and ranges support case studies of a few radiations. They do not separate isolation from the other variables that change on islands, so discriminating power stays low.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare morphological or genetic divergence of species that entered an isolated region together, as an already competing set, with divergence of species that arrived alone into new biotic relationships. The claim predicts little change in the first case and more change in the second.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relevant comparisons are spread across separate phylogeographic studies.

Whether colonists arrived together or alone is rarely recorded in a database.

Time since arrival and population size vary with isolation and can produce the same divergence pattern.

fields.value:
